## What the package is for

crimlab computes statistics that come up again and again in criminology and
sociolegal research: disparity measures for policing, the weight of forensic
evidence, clearance rates, and what can and cannot be learnt about release
rules and sentences from administrative records. Most of them are short
formulas. They are easy to get slightly wrong, and easier still to read as
showing more than they do.

Each function checks its arguments, computes the quantity in a compiled
core, and returns a plain data frame or named vector. Its help page says what
the number is and the conditions under which it means what it seems to mean.
Where the result rests on an identity or a bound, `proof()` names the
machine-checked proof of it.

The examples below use made-up numbers chosen to show the arithmetic. None of
them is data, and nothing in this vignette is an empirical finding.

```{r}
library(crimlab)
```

## Disparities: the veil of darkness

Suppose, purely for illustration, that a force recorded these traffic stops
of two groups of drivers, in daylight and in darkness:

```{r}
day <- c(white = 600, black = 400)
night <- c(white = 700, black = 300)
vodtst(day, night)
```

Black drivers are 40 per cent of daylight stops and 30 per cent of stops in
darkness. The `ratio` column compares each group's odds of being the one
stopped in daylight with its odds in darkness, against the reference group
(the first, here): about 1.56 for black drivers. The idea, due to Grogger and
Ridgeway (2006), is that an officer can see a driver's race more easily in
daylight, so if race affects who is stopped, the group it works against makes
up a larger share of daylight stops.

What this does not license: the ratio isolates the effect of visibility only
if the same people are on the road, in the same proportions, in daylight and
in darkness. If black drivers made up a larger share of daytime traffic than
of night-time traffic, the ratio would exceed 1 with no bias at all. Studies
therefore compare stops at the same clock times in different seasons, when
the same commuters drive in light and in dark. The `shift` argument shows how
much a difference in exposure would explain. If, say, black drivers' share of
traffic were 1.3 times as large in daylight as in darkness:

```{r}
vodtst(day, night, shift = c(white = 1, black = 1.3))[["adj"]]
```

the adjusted ratio is about 1.2. A shift of about 1.56 would explain the
whole contrast. The counts alone cannot tell bias from a change in who
drives; `proof("vodtst")` names the theorem that says so.

A related trap is reading an odds ratio as a relative risk. With an outcome
as common as 40 per cent, an odds ratio of 3 corresponds to a relative risk
of under 2:

```{r}
orrisk(or = 3, rate = 0.4, share = 0.5)
```

## Forensics: a match and what it is worth

Take a DNA profile typed at two loci, heterozygous at the first and
homozygous at the second, with these (illustrative) allele frequencies and a
coancestry coefficient of 0.03:

```{r}
m <- gtmp(p = c(D3 = 0.1, vWA = 0.2), q = c(0.3, NA),
          hom = c(FALSE, TRUE), theta = 0.03)
m
10^m[["log10lr"]]
```

The match probability is the chance that an unrelated person from the same
population would share the profile. Its reciprocal, about 200 here, is the
likelihood ratio for a single-source match: the profile is about 200 times as
probable if the suspect is the source as if an unrelated person is.

What this does not license: a likelihood ratio is not the probability that
the suspect is the source. That needs a prior, and the same ratio gives very
different answers under different priors:

```{r}
lrpost(lr = rep(10^m[["log10lr"]], 3), prior = c(1 / 10, 1 / 1000, 1 / 1e5))
```

Reading the ratio as the posterior is the prosecutor's fallacy. The ratio
also assumes the alternative source is unrelated to the suspect. A brother
is far more likely to share the profile; `kinidx()` gives the weight of two
profiles for a stated relationship.

How good is a system that reports likelihood ratios? Given ratios from
validation comparisons whose truth is known, the log-likelihood-ratio cost
scores them: 0 is perfect, 1 is a system that always reports 1. `cllrmin()`
splits the cost into the part due to how well the ratios separate the two
kinds of comparison (`min`) and the part due to miscalibration (`cal`):

```{r}
same <- c(50, 200, 8, 0.5)
diff <- c(0.01, 0.2, 1.5, 0.001)
cllrmin(same, diff)
```

With these made-up ratios one different-source ratio (1.5) is larger than
one same-source ratio (0.5), so even ratios perfectly calibrated to this
ordering would cost about a quarter of a bit; the rest of the cost, about
0.17 bits, comes from the ratios being too large or too small for what they
separate. With four comparisons of each kind this says nothing about any
real system; validation needs many
comparisons, made under the conditions of casework. A Tippett plot shows the
same ratios as two curves:

```{r tippett, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Tippett plot: the share of same-source and different-source likelihood ratios at or above each value of the log10 likelihood ratio."}
tipplt(same, diff)
```

## Policing: clearance rates and Simpson's paradox

Two (invented) years of offences recorded and cleared, by type:

```{r}
cl <- clrsmp(clra = c(minor = 90, serious = 20),
             reca = c(minor = 100, serious = 50),
             clrb = c(minor = 19, serious = 60),
             recb = c(minor = 20, serious = 140))
cl[["parts"]]
cl[["total"]]
```

Both types clear better in year B than in year A, yet the aggregate rate falls
from about 0.73 to about 0.49. The decomposition shows why: the rate effect
is positive, and the mix effect is negative and larger than the fall, because
recorded work moved toward serious offences, which clear less often.
`simpson` is 2 because every type moved one way and the aggregate the
other.

What this does not license: the decomposition is arithmetic on the recorded
counts. It says nothing about whether the service worked better or worse.
Clearance depends on what is recorded, how offences are classified, and what
counts as cleared, and any of these can change between years or between
services. An aggregate clearance rate compared without the split by type can
point the wrong way, as here; the split by type is only as good as the
classification.

## Corrections: what records say about a sentence

Suppose (again for illustration) 500 people, each given a community sentence
or custody, with an indicator of reconviction:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
z <- sample(c("community", "custody"), 500, replace = TRUE,
            prob = c(0.6, 0.4))
y <- rbinom(500, 1, ifelse(z == "custody", 0.55, 0.35))
sntbnd(y, z)
```

The observed reconviction rates differ by about 0.18. But each person is seen
under one sentence only. Without assumptions about who receives which
sentence, the reconviction rate everyone would have had under custody is
known only to lie within an interval as wide as the share who did not
receive custody, and the effect of custody against a community sentence lies
in an interval of width exactly 1 that contains 0 (Manski and Nagin 1998).

What this does not license: the observed difference is not the effect of the
sentence. Judges choose sentences with information about the person, so the
two groups differ before sentencing. Narrowing the interval needs an
assumption that the data cannot check, such as random assignment, and the
conclusions are only as good as that assumption.

## Proofs

`proof()` lists the theorems behind a function:

```{r}
p <- proof("clrsmp")
p
```

The files ship with the package and can be read in R or checked with Lean
(see the README). This is the statement of Kitagawa's identity, the reason
the rate and mix effects always add up to the change:

```{r}
src <- readLines(system.file(p[["file"]][1], package = "crimlab"),
                 encoding = "UTF-8")
i <- grep("^theorem kitagawa", src)
writeLines(src[i:(i + 2)])
```

A Lean proof guarantees that the theorem, exactly as stated, follows from its
hypotheses over the real numbers. It does not guarantee three other things:

* that the code is free of bugs. The C++ core uses floating-point
  arithmetic, not real numbers, and could compute something other than the
  formula proved. The package's tests check the code against the proved
  identities, which is evidence, not proof;
* that the statement is the one you need. Read it: a theorem about
  workload shares that sum to 1 says nothing about shares that do not;
* that your data meet the model's assumptions. The veil-of-darkness
  theorem holds when exposure is the same in daylight and darkness; whether
  it is for a given force and year is a question about the world, not about
  the proof.

## References

Grogger, J. and Ridgeway, G. (2006). Testing for racial profiling in traffic
stops from behind a veil of darkness. *Journal of the American Statistical
Association*, 101(475), 878-887.

Kitagawa, E. M. (1955). Components of a difference between two rates.
*Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 50(272), 1168-1194.

Manski, C. F. and Nagin, D. S. (1998). Bounding disagreements about
treatment effects: a case study of sentencing and recidivism. *Sociological
Methodology*, 28(1), 99-137.
